output.brief: The gap is mostly explained by time in level, not work location. Only 32% of remote staff had the 18 months in their current level that the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%) and approval rates (71% vs 74%) are nearly the same, and promotion rates are 20.0% vs 21.1%. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2% against the 7.6% observed. The remaining difference is small and could be chance, since only 110 remote staff are eligible. This does not rule out some proximity effect. Managers' comments hint at it, and I couldn't check stretch assignments because the staffing data doesn't record them. I'm fairly confident (~80%) that the office-attendance rule isn't justified by this evidence. It would also hit about 180 remote staff hired on home-based contracts. Next steps: hold the proposal. Report promotion rates for eligible staff only. Check the comparison again at the FY2027 cycle. Also start recording who gets stretch work, and look at why remote staff are newer, such as hiring growth or attrition.
